Health experts say it may get worse. Five probable cases were reported in Rock County. It's the third cluster of cases in Wisconsin unrelated to the outbreak in the southwest region By Hope Kirwan October 15, 2026 A nurse, prepares a combination measles, mumps and rubella vaccine for a patient at a pediatrics clinic in Easley, S.C., March 17, 2026. AP Photo/Mary Conlon, File Wisconsin health officials have identified yet another cluster of measles cases this year. The state Department of Health Services on Tuesday reported five suspected cases in Rock County. Officials are still investigating how the new infections started. But Wisconsin has already seen similar clusters of cases this year. Understanding Wisconsin, Together. WPR’s “Wisconsin Today” newsletter keeps you connected to the state you love without feeling overwhelmed. No paywall. No agenda. No corporate filter. LinkedIn This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged. Email Chippewa County now has 11 confirmed cases after first identifying one infection related to out-of-state travel in late September. In Marathon County, six cases of measles have been confirmed since a single infection from out-of-state travel was found one month ago. Of the 267 cases reported in Wisconsin this year, the vast majority have been linked to the ongoing outbreak in the southwestern region. But Dr. Jim Conway, medical director for UW Health Immunization program, said it’s not surprising that unrelated cases are popping up given the level of measles activity around the country. Since measles was declared eliminated in the U.S. in 2000, Conway said the cases that have been identified have been isolated to local outbreaks. “Because we had relatively high immunization rates, they were manageable,” he said. “What we’ve now seen over this last 18 to 24 months is this evolution, where it’s starting to act more like what we call an endemic disease, which means it’s circulating in multiple places at multiple times, and then you’re going to get these sort of spinoffs.” Conway credits state and local health officials with keeping these cases from turning into larger outbreaks by quickly and thoroughly identifying those who have been exposed to the highly-contagious virus. Measles is the most contagious infection, according to pediatric infectious disease specialist Dr. Thomas Boyce from Marshfield Clinic Health System. He said it’s five times more contagious than COVID-19, and even a small number of cases in a community can be devastating. Children under a year old, who are not eligible for the vaccine, have the highest risk of mortality from measles, he said. “Even in an area where there’s good measles vaccine uptake, if an infant or a pregnant woman or an immunocompromised person, somebody who’s had a heart transplant or is immunosuppressed in some other way, acquires measles, it can easily be fatal,” Boyce said. “Occasionally it’s fatal even in previously healthy children.” It typically takes 11 to 12 days after someone is exposed for the first symptoms to appear — what’s referred to as the incubation period. Boyce said that means an outbreak can look like more of a prolonged smolder than an out-of-control wildfire, like the recent outbreaks in Texas and Pennsylvania. Boyce said most infectious disease doctors are worried about what will happen this winter, when the spread of all respiratory viruses picks up while people are stuck indoors. “It’s certainly ripe for bigger outbreaks than what we’re seeing right now,” he said. The virus’ long incubation period also means that public health officials have to stay alert for new infections for more than a month to ensure cases aren’t continuing to spread under the radar, according to Conway. To keep a cluster of cases from turning into a full-blown outbreak, Conway said people need to make sure they’ve received two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine, especially anyone who grew up before the recommendation of two doses was adopted in 1989. “These vaccines are extraordinarily safe and are really effective,” Conway said. “These vaccines have been around since the 1970s. I mean, we know more about these vaccines than almost any other vaccine.” Individual choice over what vaccines a person or their children receive has become increasingly important to some communities since the COVID-19 pandemic. But Boyce emphasized that the choice not to vaccinate is not inconsequential. He compares it to a parent’s choice whether to use a carseat. “You can either put your child in the car seat, or you can let them ride on your lap. But I think everyone would agree that there is only one best choice to make in that situation,” he said. “I would strongly argue that with vaccines and children, there is only one best choice, and that is to vaccinate your child with the routine vaccines that are recommended by your child’s physician.” In Wisconsin communities affected by measles, opinions on vaccines remain mixed Wisconsin Public Radio, © Copyright 2026, Board of Regents of the University of Wisconsin System and Wisconsin Educational Communications Board. Photo: Erskine Palmer/CDC/Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Pennsylvania's measles outbreak has seen cases surge past 1,130 as another death linked to the disease was announced this week. Why it matters: The death of a 39-year-old woman in Franklin County last Saturday would be the sixth measles death this year in the state. Zoom in: The woman had several underlying conditions, including a diagnosis of measles with treatment, per a news release from the Franklin County coroner's office. The coroner's office said it meets the definition of a measles-related death set by the state's health department. The coroner's office tells Axios the woman was unvaccinated. What else: Stephanie Nojiri, a spokesperson for the state's Department of Health, tells Axios that it's reviewing the death in Franklin County but has yet to confirm it's measles-related. Zoom out: Pennsylvania has seen at least 1,136 cases of measles this year as of Oct. 9, which is the worst outbreak in decades. The outbreak has largely centered on Lancaster County. The latest case figures are expected to be released later today on the state's online dashboard. What else: The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention now lists two U.S. measles deaths on its website as of Tuesday, but doesn't indicate they happened in Pennsylvania. email (opens in new window) sms (opens in new window) facebook (opens in new window) twitter (opens in new window) linkedin (opens in new window) bluesky (opens in new window) nextdoor (opens in new window) Add Axios on Google More Philadelphia stories Politics Mapped: Data center pipeline in Pennsylvania Sep 28, 2026 Go deeper (<1 min. read) Things to Do Ed Sheeran tour drama comes to Philly this weekend Sep 17, 2026 Go deeper (<1 min. read) Business By the numbers: Waymo logs big miles in Philadelphia Sep 29, 2026 Go deeper (<1 min. read) Climate Nor'easter arrives in the Philly region Sep 23, 2026 Go deeper (<1 min. read) News The bell tolls for the Academy of Natural Science's museum Sep 25, 2026 Go deeper (<1 min. read) More stories Get a free daily digest of the most important news in your backyard with Axios Philadelphia. Image courtesy of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. MILWAUKEE — The Wisconsin Department of Health Services confirms new outbreaks of measles across the state, bringing the total number of confirmed cases to 267. In Rock County, health officials have reported five probable cases that are linked to one another, but the source of the infection remains unknown. The cases are listed as probable based on the appearance of symptoms, but they have not been confirmed through lab testing. Six newly confirmed cases have been reported in Marathon County along with 11 confirmed cases in Chippewa County are related to out-of-state travel. Health department officials in both of those counties are working to “identify and notify people who may have been exposed to the measles virus”. DHS official say none of the newly confirmed or probable cases are tied to outbreak in Southwest Wisconsin that is impacting Grant, Iowa, Lafayette, and Vernon counties. Those counties are currently reporting 237 confirmed and 6 probable cases that have been spreading locally. Of the state’s 267 confirmed cases, 265 (or 99.3%) of the cases were in individuals who are not vaccinated, and 5 people have been hospitalized. DHS urges all people to check their vaccination status, as vaccination against measles through two doses of the MMR vaccine is the best way to prevent measles illness. content: Skip to main content Download the AppGet your news faster with our mobile experience Install News Weather NBC3 | CBS5 | CW6 Sports Money Watch Live Now 66° Sat 46° Sun 60° Sign In or Create Account Watch Oneida County's first two confirmed measles cases in 30 years by Morgan Schaffer Mon, October 12, 2026 at 7:05 AM Updated Mon, October 12, 2026 at 10:45 AM Two measles virus cases have been reported in Oneida County over the weekend. (CREDIT: Getty Images) 11Comment Share topics: Measles Oneida County MMR vaccination Governor Hochul State of emergency MMR rates Highly contagious Health department UTICA, N.Y. — Two measles virus cases have been reported in Oneida County over the weekend. They are the first two cases of measles that the county has seen in 30 years, with the last reported case being in 1996. According to the Oneida County Health Department, both infected individuals are members of the same household and were not vaccinated against the virus before contracting it. At this time, anyone who may be at risk or were in contact with these two individuals has been contacted and there is no threat to the general public. Governor Hochul declared a state of emergency with the rising number of cases on Oct. 5. As of Oct. 6, there have been 102 reported and confirmed cases of the measles virus since the beginning of this year. Experts attribute the rise in cases in the decline in MMR vaccination rates, which helps fight against measles. The measles virus is highly contagious and can have adverse health effects on vulnerable individuals. Symptoms begin within 7 to 14 days of contracting the virus and can last up to three weeks. Symptoms of the virus include: Powered By 10 Sec 'Home for good’: Baldwinsville boy celebrates adoption Next Stay High fever (may spike to 104F) Cough Runny nose Red, watery eyes Rash (starts at hairline and spreads downward) To be fully protected against the virus, experts recommend receiving both doses of the MMR (Measles, Mumps, Rubella) vaccination. If you believe you may have contracted measles, contact your healthcare provider or emergency department before seeking care. By Ryan Hodges and Anjolina Fantaroni Published: Oct. 13, 2026 at 9:28 PM UTC|Updated: Oct. 14, 2026 at 3:19 AM UTC Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google HUNTSVILLE, Ala. (WAFF) - Alabama health officials are warning the public after a case of measles was reported in Huntsville involving an international traveler who visited businesses in the Bailey Cove area while infectious. The Alabama Department of Public Health says a private lab reported the positive test and is now urging anyone who may have been exposed to check their vaccine status and watch for symptoms. Possible exposure locations in Huntsville Health officials say the person visited these locations: Subway, 7900 Bailey Cove Road in Huntsville, on Oct. 4, 5 and 7 between 11:30 a.m. and 3 p.m. Publix at 12796 Bailey Cove Road Southeast, on Oct. 4 between 1 and 3 p.m. ADPH advises anyone who was at the restaurant or store during those times to check their vaccine status and monitor for measles symptoms. Wes Stubblefield with the ADPH said measles is a highly infectious virus. “Individuals should, if they were in proximity or in those establishments at that time, they should monitor themselves for symptoms,” Stubblefield said. “And if they have any symptoms that might be concerning for a measles illness, that they notify their local physician or any clinic that they present to before they go. Tell them that they are concerned that they may have been in contact and may have symptoms concerning for measles.” What to know about measles symptoms Measles is a serious, highly contagious viral respiratory illness that spreads through droplets in the air when someone with measles coughs or sneezes. If exposed, unvaccinated people have a 90% chance of becoming infected. Symptoms usually appear 7 to 14 days after infection, and infected people can spread it to others for several days before showing symptoms. Common symptoms include: High fever, which may spike to more than 104 degrees Cough Runny nose Red, watery eyes Rash How to protect yourself with MMR vaccine Health officials say the best way to protect yourself is to get the measles-mumps-rubella, or MMR, vaccine. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reported more than 4,000 confirmed measles cases in the U.S. this year. Many cases originate from international travel. CDC recommendations: Children: Two doses of MMR vaccine First dose at 12 through 15 months Second dose at 4 through 6 years before school entry Adults: 1 or 2 doses of MMR vaccine, depending on risk factors Anyone traveling internationally should be fully vaccinated before traveling. Infants 6 to 11 months old should get one dose before travel, then two more doses after their first birthday. Measles can cause serious complications, especially in children under 5, including ear infections, diarrhea, pneumonia, swelling of the brain and even death. Parents should make sure their children are up to date on routine immunizations. Adults unsure of their status should contact their health care provider. content: Accessibility links Skip to main content Keyboard shortcuts for audio player Open Navigation Menu Newsletters NPR Shop Get NPR+ Close Navigation Menu Home News Expand/collapse submenu for News National World Politics Business Elections Health Science Climate Race Culture Expand/collapse submenu for Culture Books Movies Television Pop Culture Food Art & Design Performing Arts Life Kit Gaming Music Expand/collapse submenu for Music Tiny Desk New Music Friday All Songs Considered Music Features Live Sessions Podcasts & Shows Expand/collapse submenu for Podcasts & Shows Daily Morning Edition Weekend Edition Saturday Weekend Edition Sunday All Things Considered Up First Here & Now NPR Politics Podcast Featured Wait Wait...Don't Tell Me! Fresh Air Wild Card with Rachel Martin It's Been a Minute Machine Gods Get NPR+ More Podcasts & Shows Search Newsletters NPR Shop Get NPR+ Tiny Desk New Music Friday All Songs Considered Music Features Live Sessions About NPR Diversity Support Careers Press Ethics Do adults need another measles shot? Vaccination is the best way to protect yourself against measles. For most adults, one shot of the MMR is considered enough protection. But there are certain situations that call for a second dose. Special Series Living Better Science for a healthy life Here's what to know if you're unsure about your measles immunity status October 12, 20265:00 AM ET Heard on Morning Edition Maria Godoy Do adults need another measles shot? Listen · 3:24 3:24 Transcript Toggle more options Download Embed Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5991904/nx-s1-9960895" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player"> Transcript Maria Fabrizio for NPR Measles is the most contagious disease known. It can rip through a population without immunity like wildfire. Just look at what's happening in Pennsylvania, says Patsy Stinchfield, executive director of the Measles Collaborative, a public health effort led by the National Foundation for Infectious Diseases. Health As diseases loom, CDC's response to measles deaths stirs fears about agency's reliability "In January in Pennsylvania, they had 12 cases. Now we're seeing 100 plus cases per week and over 1,000 cases in Pennsylvania," she says. "If Pennsylvania can see it spread that fast, that can happen in any state that has low immunization rates." As vaccination rates have fallen across the country, many communities have become vulnerable. Nationwide, more than 4,000 measles cases have been reported this year alone — the highest number in 35 years. Pennsylvania has reported five deaths. New York state declared a measles emergency. Stinchfield says the recent measles surge has got many people wondering if they're at risk. "It's a very common question for people to ask, 'am I immune? Am I OK? What do I need to do?' And that is exactly the right question everyone should be asking themselves right now," Stinchfield says. The best defense is vaccination. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is 97% effective — meaning 97% of people will have an immune response. "The measles vaccine is safe. It's highly effective, and it confers lifelong immunity," says Dr. Adam Ratner, a pediatric infectious disease physician in New York City and author of Booster Shots, a history of measles. Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter. But what if you don't know your immunization history, or you only got one dose of the measles shot? Should you get another dose? Infectious disease experts say that depends on several factors. If you were born before 1957 People born before 1957 are presumed to be immune because back then, measles was so common, just about everyone got it in childhood, says Dr. Larry Kociolek, a pediatric infectious disease specialist at Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago and an associate professor of pediatrics at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine. "It was thought that pretty much everyone in the U.S. was infected with measles as sort of a rite of passage in childhood," Kocielek says. He says anyone who's ever had measles can be confident they're protected. That is of course, if you survived. Before vaccines, measles used to kill 400 to 500 people each year in the U.S. Maria Fabrizio for NPR If you were vaccinated before 1968 People who were born after 1957 and vaccinated before 1968 may need an additional dose. That's because a small group of people who were immunized during that time received an early, less effective version of the vaccine that used inactivated or killed virus. If you're not sure which vaccine you got, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends talking to your doctor about getting one or two doses of the MMR vaccine. If you only got one dose of the MMR vaccine At first, children in the U.S. received just one dose of the MMR vaccine. But that changed in 1989, after public health officials determined that a single dose wasn't enough to prevent outbreaks. That year, the official recommendation switched to two doses of MMR vaccine for children, which is still in effect today. Health An early flu season means it might be time to think about a flu shot Kids need the higher protection "because they tend to be at higher risk of exposure, since they're oftentimes in group settings like schools and daycares," Kociolek says. If you're in a higher-risk group One dose of MMR vaccine is 93% effective, and traditionally, Kociolek says, that was considered enough protection for most adults, unless they were at higher risk of being exposed to measles. Health care workers, people in a college setting and those travelling abroad are all in this group. If you live with or are in close contact with someone who is immunocompromised, you also need two doses of vaccine to protect them. But given the recent, dramatic rise of measles across the country these days, "if you are living in areas with high measles activity, it does make a whole lot of sense for adults to go ahead and get that second dose," Kociolek says. Ratner says it's definitely worth asking your doctor if you should get a second dose. While measles is often considered to be a childhood disease, a large proportion of people sickened this year have been unvaccinated adults — and people over 20 who lack immunity are at higher risk of serious complications. No matter your age, "measles is a serious disease," Stinchfield says. She notes that getting two doses of the vaccine can also help others at higher risk who can't get the MMR shot, including people who are pregnant, severely immunocompromised and infants under 6 months of age. Maria Fabrizio for NPR If you really don't know your immunization history If you're just not sure if you're protected against measles and you can't find records of immunization, you could get a test to check your blood antibody levels. But those tests aren't perfect, says Dr. William Moss, a professor of epidemiology at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. Living Better Travel plans? Here's what to know as measles exposures reach trains and games "It's possible that a person could actually be protected and test negative on one of those," Moss says. Depending on your circumstances, your insurance might not cover the blood test. But most private insurance plans and Medicaid must cover another MMR vaccine at no cost. Moss says if you can't confirm how many doses of MMR vaccine you've had, "I would say it is easier and less expensive to just get another MMR vaccine, and there is no harm in getting a second MMR vaccine or even a third, additional MMR dose." After all, it's much better to be protected than infected. NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. content_title: 39-year-old unvaccinated woman becomes 6th measles death in Pennsylvania
content: A 39-year-old unvaccinated woman in Franklin County, Pennsylvania, has become the sixth person to die of the highly infectious virus amid a state outbreak that has stricken over a thousand people since it began in April. The woman died on Saturday, October 10. She had several underlying health conditions and had recently tested positive for measles, according to an advisory posted on social media by Franklin County Coroner Jordan Conner. The advisory noted that the woman’s death meets the definition of a measles death set by the state’s health department. In an emailed statement to The Washington Post , the coroner’s office said the primary cause of death was listed as “probable acute cardiac event due to possible complications of the measles.” The previous five deaths amid the state’s measles outbreak included a newborn , a 6-week-old , an 18-year-old , a 20-year-old , and a 40-year-old . All the deceased were unvaccinated; the two infants were too young to have been vaccinated. Ars Video As of the latest measles update from Pennsylvania’s health department on Friday, October 9, there have been 1,136 cases in the state since the start of the year—1,124 of which are from the current outbreak. Overall, 218 people have been hospitalized. The outbreak, which now spans 41 of the state’s 67 counties, shows no signs of slowing. There had been 157 new cases reported just in the previous week. A spokesperson for the state health department told the Post that it is “aware” of the new death and is reviewing the case. It will provide an update once the review is complete. Measles, declared eliminated in the US in 2000, is roaring back amid misinformation and slipping vaccination rates. The nationwide measles case count for the year has hit 4,080 , the highest total since 1991. Pennsylvania’s outbreak is also the largest on record since that year . The US is widely expected to lose its measles elimination status when experts from the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) meet in November to review US measles data. Under anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has only included two of the six deaths so far in its reporting. There were three measles deaths reported in the US in 2025. Prior to those deaths, there had not been a measles death reported in the country since 2015. Beth Mole Senior Health Reporter Beth Mole Senior Health Reporter Beth is Ars Technica’s Senior Health Reporter. Beth has a Ph.D. in microbiology from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and attended the Science Communication program at the University of California, Santa Cruz. She specializes in covering infectious diseases, public health, and microbes. 213 Comments

(WSAZ) - One case of measles has been confirmed in Pike County, Ohio according to a press release from the Pike County General Health District on October 8, 2026. As of October 8, 2026, the CDC says there are 147 confirmed cases of measles in the state of Ohio. The Pike County General Health District says measles is a highly contagious viral illness that can spread easily. The virus can live in the air for up to two hours after an infected person leaves. Some symptoms of measles include a high fever, cough, runny nose, watery or red eyes, and potentially a rash that could begin three to five days after symptoms appear. People who have symptoms of measles should avoid contact with others and immediately contact their health care provider. Copyright 2026 WSAZ. All rights reserved.
